 ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner’s hometown 
 Schreiner was a first-round NFL draft pick before he joined the Marines near the end of World War II and was sent into battle in the Pacific. By Ashley Weil Published : Nov. 1, 2026 at 8:34 PM CST Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - More than 100 people nearly filled the Grantland Theater on Sunday afternoon to watch “The Mosquito Bowl,” a movie inspired by the life of Dave Schreiner, an All-American player at the University of Wisconsin from Lancaster.
 Schreiner was a first-round NFL draft pick before he joined the Marines near the end of World War II and was sent into battle in the Pacific. 
 The movie, inspired by his life and others, is showing in select theaters ahead of its Netflix release.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) Families fill the theater
 Families packed the Grantland Theater to see the film, which tells his story, which began in Lancaster.
 “I think it’s a good thing for Lancaster, because it is a town where people care about each other,” Linda Lucke, president of the board of directors for the Grant County Historical Society, said.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) Among those in attendance was Schreiner’s niece, Judy Corfield. 
 Corfield said she was two when Schreiner left for the war and three and a half when he died.
 “I don’t have memories so much as what I’ve been told,” she said. “I happened to be living in Lancaster at the time that the telegram came.”
 Corfield said it has been emotional to see on screen a story she has heard her whole life.
 “I think my mother and my grandmother and my family would be very pleased,” she said.
 Corfield said she has seen the film twice.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) “Tears first. But having seen it twice, now I can appreciate it better,” she said.
 Corfield said she hopes viewers take away the message of the story.
 “The story tells from the football field to the battlefield and what teamwork and bonding and camaraderie is about,” she said. “And I think that’s what I would like people to take away from it.”
 Corfield said author Buzz Bissinger, who wrote the book “The Mosquito Bowl,” had access to Schreiner’s letters and photographs from childhood through his war letters.
 “I think the movie portrays him the way my family would appreciate, the way he was,” she said.
 Judy Corfield at The Mosquito Bowl Premier (Judy Corfield) She said Netflix invited her to Quantico to see the first showing of the film and to the premiere in Hollywood, where she met the stars and the director.
 She described it as “a very unique experience and very special.”
 Judy Corfield at The Mosquito Bowl Premier (Judy Corfield) Museum displays items from Schreiner’s life
 The Grant County History Museum features items from Schreiner’s life.
 Lucke said the museum has had some of Schreiner’s artifacts on permanent display for some time and added items after it learned about the movie. She said his military items are also on display. 
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) She said his story is an example for young people.
 “Somebody from a small town can still make a difference in the world big time,” Lucke said.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) Corfield said her grandmother and mother donated items from the family home to the museum, including a crib that she said the children were born in and slept in.
 “My grandmother was a keeper and she put these scrapbooks together, and I understand they have several more of everything that David did all through his life,” Corfield said.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) She said she plans to donate Schreiner’s letter sweater. Corfield said she found a ticket in the pocket from the Oct. 7, 2006, game when Wisconsin played Northwestern. She said she last wore the sweater at that game, when Schreiner’s name went on the inside of Camp Randall Stadium.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) Corfield also pointed to the house in Lancaster where the family grew up.
 “This is the house that they built in 1915,” she said.
 Corfield said Lancaster is a place she has returned to all her life. Her grandparents lived there, she said, and she visited them every summer. She said her parents and the rest of the Shriner family are buried there.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) Corfield said her grandparents set up a scholarship fund at the University of Wisconsin when Schreiner died. The fund is now known as the Shriner Hoskins Scholarship Fund.
 “I still get thank you letters from people receiving that scholarship,” Corfield said.
 Historical society and the screenings
 Lucke said the Grant County Historical Society is a nonprofit, all-volunteer organization that has existed for 75 years or more. 
 She said it operates the museum, the Genealogy Research Center next door and the Mitchell Rountree Stone Cottage in Platteville. She said the society is looking for volunteers.
 “We’re trying to make history important,” Lucke said.
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) Lucke said only the main level of the museum is accessible to people with disabilities. She said the museum wants to add a limited-use elevator so it can add hands-on exhibits on the lower level and store artifacts that are now kept in the building next door.
 “I would just like to invite people to come see our corner of the world,” Lucke said. “I think it’s one of the best-kept secrets in Wisconsin.”
 'The Mosquito Bowl' draws crowd to Lancaster theater in Dave Schreiner's hometown (WMTV) The Grantland Theater is showing the film through Nov. 5.
 A question-and-answer session was held Sunday following the screening.
 The Grant County History Museum has extended its hours this week for people coming to see the film. It is open Tuesday through Thursday from 1 to 6 p.m.
